title: Jubilee 2000
hook: churches campaigned to cancel poor countries' debts, citing Leviticus 25

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hospice: Cicely Saunders, and a place built to keep watch with the dying. Your line was you matter to the end.

Fifty years, then a trumpet. In the book of Leviticus, Israel is told to count seven times seven years, and then, on the day of atonement, to sound the trumpet through the whole land. What follows is a startling law. A field sold in a bad year goes back to the family that lost it. People who had sold themselves into service go home. Much later, churches and aid groups picked up that trumpet and pointed it at something modern: the debts weighing on poor countries. They named their campaign after the old law.

The law is in Leviticus 25. The fiftieth year is holy, and the King James Bible gives the command: "proclaim liberty throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof: it shall be a jubile unto you." The reason comes a few verses on, spoken by God: "for the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me." Nobody owns the ground forever. Everyone is a guest on it. Wealth can pile up for a while, but not for good. Deuteronomy has a smaller cousin of the idea: "At the end of every seven years thou shalt make a release," a letting go of debts between neighbors. The honest part: some readers note that the rest of the Bible tells no story of a jubilee being kept. The idea traveled anyway. In Luke, Jesus reads from Isaiah in his hometown and announces "the acceptable year of the Lord," and some readers hear a jubilee in it. Christians who pray the Lord's Prayer in Matthew's words say: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Christian groups, joined by people of other faiths and none, argued that old loans were pressing on countries that could barely pay for their own clinics and schools, and that a fresh start was owed. They gathered signatures, held vigils and marched. Some debts were later written off; others were not, and people still argue about what helped. But a line from an ancient law about farmland had walked into the rooms where finance ministers meet.
screen: `THE LAND IS MINE: YOU ARE GUESTS.`
`AN OLD LAW IN THE FINANCE MINISTRY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a debt, not only money, that has sat on the table a long time, and hold it without adding it up; then widen the circle to a country carrying something it cannot lift. If you pray, you can pray the line from Matthew, forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors; if you don't, just let the word release sit with you.
Jubilee. The fiftieth year in Leviticus, when debts were let go and lost land went home, the ancient law that named a modern campaign to cancel poor countries' debts.
Your line: proclaim liberty. The field goes home, and the land stays God's. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian aid groups campaign and pray for debt relief for poor countries, often drawing on the jubilee of Leviticus 25 and the line "forgive us our debts" from the Lord's Prayer.

fork.reveal: Leviticus 25: in the jubilee, every man returns to his possession. the reason given is surprising: the land was never anyone's to sell forever. "the land is mine."

what a scholar hears: Leviticus gives the law, and some readers note no story of it being kept. the idea travels on anyway, into Luke 4, the Lord's Prayer, and a modern campaign about debt.

chat.says: Why do people call canceling poor countries' debts a jubilee? Isn't that just a party?
options: It's from Leviticus: every fiftieth year, debts were let go and lost land went home.
It's from the Gospels: Jesus threw a feast where everyone's debts were paid off.
It's an old royal custom, when kings forgave taxes to celebrate a long reign.
chat.meaning: In Leviticus 25 the fiftieth year proclaims liberty: lost land goes home and people go free. Debt-relief campaigners named their call after it.

notes: Claims rule: 'seven times seven years', 'fiftieth year' and 'the day of atonement' are from Leviticus 25:8–10 directly. No dates, counts of signatures, countries or amounts of debt are given for the campaign.

Liberty Bell: the bell carries the Leviticus 25:10 line ('Proclaim LIBERTY Throughout all the Land unto all the Inhabitants thereof Lev. XXV X.'). This is not in the cited text; confirm it may stay, or cut.
'the Bible never describes Israel actually celebrating one': the standard scholarly observation (Jeremiah 34 concerns a seventh-year release of slaves, not a jubilee). Confirm wording.
'some readers hear a jubilee in it' (Luke 4:19): attributed, not stated as fact. Confirm.

Campaign summary kept general: churches and aid groups, people of other faiths and none, signatures, vigils, marches; 'some debts were later written off, others were not' and ongoing argument. Confirm fair; the campaign's specific outcomes (e.g. HIPC, MDRI) are deliberately not named.
Original: יוֹבֵל (yovel). Its link to the ram's horn is left out under the etymology rule.
